en: Pushing the passed pawn: the most natural move in the world — and here the decisive mistake (verified: the position drops from won to drawn). Every pawn tempo is a tempo the black king spends running for a8.
The black king dashes for the saving corner — one more step and the classic fortress (see "The Wrong Bishop") would be unbreakable.
The second and final stone of the wall: the king covers b7 (and c7), the bishop covers b8. The black king is locked OUT — b8 and b7, its only two doors to a8, are boarded up for good.

NOW the pawn may march — the point of the whole course: the very same push, played before the wall, only drew. Move order is the entire difference between winning and watching the black king settle into a8.
The black king may camp on c8, one square from the corner: it does NOT touch a8. The bishop's colour never mattered — the pawn promotes on a square nobody contests.

A queen, plain and simple. Remember the rule in both directions: wrong bishop + rook's pawn = draw IF the defending king reaches the corner — and a race to the corner otherwise. The Bf4+Kb6 wall is how that race is won.
The black king races for the corner — and nothing can stop it now: the bishop never had time to seal b8.
Through the b8 door, and the story is over. Note that this king only took two steps — the fortress really was just one race away.

The exact position of "The Wrong Bishop" course: king glued to the light corner, dark-squared bishop helpless, stalemate lying in ambush the moment White's king steps closer. An iron draw. A single move order separated this half point from the main chapter's queen.

Bishop and rook's pawn against a lone king: normally a trivial win. But if the bishop does NOT control the promotion square, the whole game can shrink to one corner and two squares — and nothing, absolutely nothing, will ever change that.
The two-square fortress

The bishop on d2 controls ONLY dark squares — never a8, where the pawn must queen. A bishop one square over (e2, light squares) would win in five moves; here, watch the black king: he needs only two squares, a8 and b8, to hold FOREVER.
The white king approaches — he may come, he can do nothing once there.
The bishop tries another diagonal: they all look the same once none of them touches a8. The black king doesn't even need to think — he shuttles between his only two squares until the end of time.
A rare, tricky countergambit: instead of defending e5, strike with …d5. Objectively dubious, but few opponents know the correct refutation.

If White plays 2.Bc4
Without 2.Nf3 there is no Elephant Gambit: the e5 pawn is not attacked, so …d5 gains no tempo. One White player in nine, and the course had nothing.
The Elephant Gambit: offer the centre for fast development and complications.
White's most solid move, played in one game in five, and the course started from 3.exd5. They take the pawn and make ours pointless.
Keep e5 strong and develop aggressively, ready for …e4 to chase the knight.
Kick the f3-knight at once; d5 must then be regained accurately.
One White player in three simply develops instead of pushing d4, and the course only planned for d4. It is the most awkward reply: they keep the pawn without committing.
The most disappointing move for us: White simply keeps the pawn and offers no target. One White player in six, missing from the course.
The knight jumps to the centre rather than retreat — nearly one White player in three, and the course only saw Qe2. On d4 it is active, but it is also a target.
Going home: humiliating in appearance, very solid in reality. One White player in five plays it, and the course said nothing about it.
We recapture in the centre. The position stays playable, but the initiative the gambit promised is gone — the price of a clean decline.
We develop while hitting d5. Play must be fast and concrete: the pawn is gone, only the initiative can pay for it.
We take the pawn back at once: the queen is safe in the centre because the d4 knight blocks White's own pieces from reaching her.
The queen steps aside while holding e4 — that advanced pawn is our only gain from the gambit; losing it would be losing everything.
They defend everything. The reality has to be accepted: against an opponent who plays simply, the Elephant Gambit gives nothing beyond being a pawn down.
We switch to a sound defence rather than force a gambit that no longer makes sense. Knowing when to drop your pet weapon is part of a repertoire.
A hypermodern flank opening: control d5 from afar and keep total flexibility. Often a Sicilian with an extra tempo.

Claiming d5 without committing the central pawns: flexible play.
Black grabs the centre: it's a Sicilian with colours reversed, White a tempo up.
The Symmetrical: both sides mirror. White looks to break the symmetry at the right moment.
The most common reply to 1.c4, and the course started from …e5 or …c5.
The most natural developing move, missing from the chapter, which started from …Nf6.
A common club move: the bishop develops fast, but it will have to move again once d4 comes.
The fianchetto is the right way to handle Black's centre: we do not hit it head-on, we watch it from afar on g2.
The reversed Dragon: White plays the Sicilian structure a tempo up.
Full symmetry. The chapter only knew …Nc6 — yet one Black player in nine develops this knight first.
Black prepares …d5 before developing a knight. Same family as the previous line, different order — and the course had nothing.
The start of a King's Indian or a Sicilian, depending on what follows. Black keeps everything open; it is up to us to take the centre while they hesitate.
One Black player in six develops this knight instead of fianchettoing, and the first batch only planned for …g6.
Black prepares …d5 without committing. Same family as the previous line, one move order earlier.
The start of a Closed Sicilian, colours reversed. The first batch only saw …g6.
The right moment to break: d4 shatters the symmetry and opens the g2 bishop.
Black is heading for a King's Indian. We can decline it by taking the centre at once.
Black takes the centre: this is a Sicilian with colours reversed, and a spare tempo for us. The chapter only planned for …e6 and …g6.
The Mikenas Attack: White seizes the whole centre. Play turns concrete at once.
The most critical reply: hit e4 immediately.
A deliberate transposition: the English turns into a queen's pawn game, where our c4 pawn already stands ideally.
Three Black players in four play this fianchetto — it IS the answer to the English — and the chapter only knew 3…d5. We enter a King's Indian, where we are the ones who took the centre first.
Pressure on d5 before castling: the idea that sets the tone for the whole line.
Fianchetto: this is a Sicilian with an extra tempo. The g2 bishop will bite on d5 all game.
Two Black players in five develop like this, and the first batch only had …g6. They build a classical centre; we will take it from the side.
Black slows b4 down. We play d4 anyway: the c5 bishop loses time, and that's our edge.
The full centre, while we can. The g7 bishop has just taken aim along a diagonal we close before it ever gets to use it.
More than four Black players in five castle here — by far the most played move in the whole repertoire — and the first batch went straight on to …e5.
We close, and it is a choice: the game becomes a battle of wings, White pushing on the queenside and Black on the kingside. Our c4 pawn is already there, theirs is not.
Black must stop h5, otherwise the h-file opens before their own attack ever gets going.
Both sides have their centre. The difference is the tempo: our pieces reach every useful square half a beat earlier.
Against symmetry, whoever breaks first and profitably takes the initiative. The g2 bishop prepares d4 under the right conditions.
The break. Black is left with an isolated pawn on d5; we get a strong square on d4 and a bishop fixing it from g2.
Black declines the isolated pawn by pushing. The c4 pawn advances far from its friends: it looks annoying, it will mostly be weak.
The isolated pawn gives Black active squares: do not think the position wins itself — it is simply easier to play for us.
Without waiting: Black has no piece contesting d4 yet, and after the trade we get a Maroczy Bind Sicilian as White — one of the best bargains in the opening.
Before closing the centre, we pin: the f6 knight guards e4 and d5, and disturbing it now is worth more than later.
The bishop goes home rather than trade itself off. Black has spent …h6 for nothing, and that loosened pawn becomes a target when we attack.
The same break as ever: we play it when it leaves Black with an isolated pawn, never before.
A modest and dangerous move: it prepares d4 in one go, with the e3 pawn behind it — the break then comes without concessions.
The bishop eyes f2, the softest square of White's castled position. That is the real venom of the Reversed Sicilian: f2 is guarded only by the king.
A pawn offered right away for queenside trickery. Dubious against precise defence, but lethal against an unwarned opponent.

The Englund Gambit: offer e5 to set queenside traps.
White declines the pawn and closes the centre. The gambit is gone: play the position, not the idea.
If White defends e5 calmly, aim to regain it without overreaching.
One White player in five develops like this rather than clinging to the pawn. Recapturing on e5 is sound but costs the initiative — the price of a cleanly declined gambit.
Gobble b2: beware the trap if White plays carelessly.
The mistake we're waiting for: the bishop defends b2 but steps onto the a1 rook's diagonal.
Forced: 8.Qxc3?? loses on the spot to 8…Qc1 mate.
The rook hangs and NOTHING defends it: we take it with check. That is the whole point of the trap.
The only block that holds — and the black queen is not trapped for all that.
A rook and two pawns for nothing: Black is winning.
Here we take back on f4, NOT b2: 5…Qxb2 leaves White clearly better after Bd2.
The coming fork on c7 looks scary — it only wins a rook that gets stranded on a8.
The a8 knight is trapped: …b6 and …Bb7 round it up. Material is level and the position playable.
The bishop takes the most active diagonal while the centre is blocked — what remains of the gambit's spirit.
We regain the material, but the f3 trade damages our own development. Know this: here the gambit yields nothing, and you must play a level position patiently.
Sound symmetrical development: all four knights come out, then choose between the quiet Spanish (Bb5), opening the centre (Scotch) or chaos (Halloween).

vs the Petrov — 2…Nf6
Black sidesteps the Four Knights by defending e5 with a pawn. The course had no answer.
The Petrov: Black does not defend e5, they counterattack. One player in ten, and the course only planned for …Nc6 and …d6.
More than a quarter of games, and the course didn't mention it. The bishop on c5 leaves a weakness: the e5 pawn has only one defender.
Black steers into a Philidor instead of developing the second knight. One player in ten, and the course only saw …Nf6 and …Bc5.
The Spanish version: perfect symmetry. White plays the structure and the Metger unpin.
Opening the centre: open, active play where White keeps a slight initiative.
The Halloween Gambit: sacrifice a knight to chase Black's pieces and grab a monster centre.
The quiet defence: three Black players in ten prop up e5 instead of pinning with …Bb4, and the course only knew that pin.
The bishop to c5 rather than b4: more active, but it leaves e5 without an extra defender. One Black player in four, missing from the course.
One Black player in three trades here, and the course only planned for …Bb4. It is a premature simplification: it opens the d-file for US.

THE move that refutes the gambit, played by nearly half of Black players. The knight retreats where d4-d5 no longer hits it. Know this before you leap: the Halloween is a surprise weapon, not a sound line.
The classic fork trick: we take, and if …Nxe5 then d4 regains the piece, hitting bishop and knight at once.
The only move: retreating to b6 or b4 would lose to d5 or dxe5.
Strike at once: the Philidor suffers from a lack of space, and this is the moment to remind it.
We open while they are still passive: the b5 bishop's pin on the c6 knight makes this break especially awkward for them.
And here is the punishment: e5 is now defended only once. With the c6 knight pinned, recapturing will cost Black something.
The queen reaches the centre and cannot be evicted — the two black knights that might have done it are gone or elsewhere.
Castling long: opposite kings, the d-file already open for our rook, and a ready-made attack in the centre and on the queenside.
The immediate break, as always against a passive defence: Black has nothing with which to contest the centre.
The forced move, and the trap to know: recapturing at once with …Nxe4 loses the queen to Qe2. Kick the knight first, recapture second.
Solid and combative: Black concedes a little space to strike the centre with …c5 and …f6. The one problem piece, the light-squared bishop, shapes the whole plan.

2.Nf3 — White avoids d4
Nearly a third of games, and the course always started from 2.d4. White keeps the centre flexible, often to dodge French theory.
The Advance: White closes the centre. Black will besiege the d4 base.
The Tarrasch: more flexible, it sidesteps the …Bb4 pin.
The exchange frees Black's problem bishop: the position becomes symmetrical and easy to play.
The Winawer: pin the c3 knight to disrupt White's centre.
The Rubinstein: give up the centre for a solid, weakness-free position.
The centre closes; the fight will be about the d4-e5 pawn chain.
White has the bishop pair, Black has doubled pawns to attack: double-edged play.
The critical move: the queen hits g7 and tests Black's king.
The Poisoned Pawn line: give up g7 to grab c3 and d4 in return.
The safe version: castle instead of grabbing the poisoned pawn.
Each side devours the other's wing: play balances on a knife's edge.
The typical break: hitting d4 at its root.
One White player in five develops instead of propping up d4 with c3, and the course only planned for c3. The d4 pawn is then underdefended.
The queen eyes b2 and above all d4: the pressure mounts.
The bishop develops BEFORE …c4 closes things: that's the nuance separating this move order from the classical French, where it often stays shut in.
The Milner-Barry Gambit: White gives up d4 to attack the king stuck in the centre.
The knight routes via h6 to land on f5 and hit d4/e3.
Grabbing d4 is fine, but precise defence must follow.
Strike the centre at once: an isolated queen's pawn arises, to be played actively.
The closed version: more strategic, with a later …f6 to undermine e5.
The Steinitz: White grabs space; Black hits back with …c5 and …f6.
